Question: How common is the use of alliteration in Chinese poetry?
Answer: Alliterations are not that common in Chinese poetry. In roughly the 3rd or 4th century ce, they started setting forms for poetry. By the Tang, say around the 7th century ce, set forms were usually used: so many words in each line, with the tones for each position established (平仄), and the rhyming pattern set. Also, I’d like to point out that, especially since about the 3rd century, poems are mercifully brief. You don’t get those monsters (as in English poetry) that go on for pages and pages. You can have a complete, polished poem in twenty syllables. It’s not easy! (Before that, especially during the Han and a while after, they had a form of poetry called 賦 fu, that does go on for pages. Fu used especially ornate vocabulary. My theory is that in the Han, to be an official, you had to memorize 9,000 characters, so if you’ve memorized them, you may as well use them. In Chinese, they have a special beauty, from the forms of the characters. I don’t think there’s any way to translate it. Aside: everybody celebrates Double Fifth but nobody really pays much attention to old Ch’ü/Qu Yuan from about 300bce and his works, so every Double Fifth, I chant his great poem 離騷 Li Sao. It takes about half an hour, so you can see it is quite long. But later poetry was much shorter.) Poetry is not my focus, but I can’t really think of any famous poems that use alliteration.

Question: How can I become a great philosopher?
Answer: That depends on what you call a “great philosopher.” Academic philosophers study logic, which is fine, but a lot of them seem to think that life can be reduced to a bunch of mathematical symbols. That’s fine, they’re harmless, they get their tenure and publish papers, and the world ignores them, because that stuff is reaaalllly dry. Example: A while back I read a paper by a very highly esteemed English academic philosopher about donating and charity. It went on for twenty pages. By the time I finished, I was numb from the cascade of terms and jargon, and had not the least intention to donate anything to charity. Then there’s a nun in Taiwan, 證嚴法師 Chengyen, who really doesn’t say much more than platitudes, but has inspired millions of people to donate time and money. Her organization, Tzu Chi, has chapters in 68 countries. My point here is that academic philosophy is sterile. So. You may know what Socrates had to say about this. “By all means marry. If you get a good wife, you'll be happy. If you get a bad one, you'll become a philosopher.” Reading books to expand your views is important, but although reading books provides an indispensable foundation, it does not make a philosopher. To become a philosopher, you have to be knocked flat, dragged through pig manure, dropped on your head, stripped of your dignity, and learn how to come through unruffled. To me, at least, what results is the only worthwhile philosophy. IMHO, becoming a philosopher is not a matter of choice. A monk, call him Chuan X, under the monk 上廣下欽老和尚 Kuangch’in/ Guangqin (1892 — 1986) told him, ‘I am encumbered by my ego, I need your help to cut down my ego.’ 幫我去我執. The master nodded and ignored him. About a week later, when all the monks and nuns were assembled, Kuangchin calmly discussed the personality of Chuan X in detail, warts and all. When the assembly was over, Chuan X packed his things and headed out the door. Kuangchin asked, ‘Where are you going?’ Chuan X said, ‘You laid my soul bare to the whole temple, I have no face, how can I stay?’ Kuangchin said, ‘But you asked for my help in cutting down your ego.’
